newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania "working flat out" for June 29 poll.
newsitem.headline: Albania "working flat out" for June 29 poll.

text.p: Albania's election authority intensified efforts at the weekend to prepare for a June 29 poll, with the government insisting there would be no delay despite signs work was falling behind schedule.
"We are working flat out for the elections which we know will be held on June 29," a spokesman at the central election commission said by telephone from the office on Sunday.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino at the weekend urged local government representatives to find ways to meet the conditions for elections in June, even threatening to sack those unable to organise the process in their areas.

Overseas observers, returning to Tirana after a week in both the north and south of this chaotic Balkan country, voiced several concerns which they said may justify a technical delay, but added that this was politically out of the question.
Snap elections aim to restore calm after violence and unrest swept through Albania following the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes earlier this year.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is helping Albania's multi-party government of national reconciliation to organise the poll, but the government has final responsibility.
Conditions for the vote, in Europe's poorest country, are far from ideal: OSCE spokesman Jeff Murray said last week the assignment was the toughest the organisation had ever had.
Parts of Albania spun out of government control in spring, and there are still patches both in the north and south where the security of candidates, voters or election observers is not guaranteed.
A multinational protection force of 6,500 mainly Italian troops is in place to help ensure the safety of observers, but cannot offer blanket coverage.
"We're trying to do this too fast," one OSCE observer told Reuters on condition of anonymity. "We couldn't do this (organise an election so quickly) in our own homes."
Observer concerns at the weekend focused on problems with the formation of regional election commissions and delays in posting voter lists.
"There will be elections in some form, but only by skipping some procedures," said the observer, discussing the north.
By last Friday, some individuals nominated by political parties to form local commissions in Albania's 115 electoral zones had not shown up, observers and local media said.
If local commissions do not succeed in forming a broad-based quorum of Albania's political spectrum, they risk a legal challenge after the poll.
"Apparently some don't want to do the job," said another observer, also requesting anonymity, after a week in the south.
Voter lists, which should have been posted by around June 12-13, were hard to find on Sunday even in the capital.

"In many cases they are producing new lists from scratch," said the observer from the north. This was not always necessary but could be lucrative for officials paid a small fee for each name they take down.
Long delays in posting voter lists could mean excluded voters do not have enough time to register, observers said.
In parts of the north, up to 40 percent of the population are registered but absent -- for instance working casually in Tirana, the northern observer added.
"That means there are large numbers of names on the list who are not there," the observer said. This could invite manipulation.
The observers said a plan to stamp each voter's wrist with indelible ink, invisible to the eye, may help solve some voter identification problems.

But there was wide concern at the election authority's plan to leave the polls open until around nightfall at nine pm, with some political parties and observers arguing a six pm closure would help prevent manipulation and boost voter security.
